description: We are vod0laz1, a team of five students from the Architectural and Engineering Collegium A+ in Kyiv, Ukraine: Matvii (team owner, front-end developer), Maksym (team captain), Dmytro (structural engineer), Denys (designer) and Stanislav (back-end developer).
summary: Asklepios is health-monitoring software for a crew flying to Mars, where a doctor's reply takes up to 44 minutes round trip and contact can drop for about two weeks. It tracks every indicator the challenge names: heart rate, blood pressure and body temperature from (simulated) wearable sensors, compared with each astronaut's own baseline, plus a daily check-in for sleep, mood and blood sugar with color-coded 7-day trends. A four-step exam turns a complaint typed in plain English or Ukrainian into an explained decision: urgency, weighted evidence, treatment steps, medicines from the onboard kit and an automatic re-check. Training alarms, a whole-mission pharmacy forecast and an autonomous crew guardian round out a design mapped to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight. It is one HTML file with zero network requests, because on the way to Mars help must already be on board.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Asklepios is an onboard medic for a four-person crew on day 214 of an 860-day Mars mission. It works without the internet and without a server, in English and Ukrainian.

- Monitoring: pulse, SpO2 and body temperature every second for each person, plus blood pressure, breathing rate, module CO2 and each person's daily radiation dose. Caution and alarm limits are computed from each person's own baseline.

- Daily check-in: once per mission day each crew member records sleep, mood and blood sugar; a reminder shows who has not checked in; the medical card shows color-coded 7-day trends.

- Exam in four steps: Patient - Complaints - Questions - Decision. Complaints are typed in plain words; the parser understands negations ("no nausea") and clauses.

- Explained decision: one of four urgency levels, a "Why" line with every piece of evidence and its weight, a step checklist, medicines from the onboard kit and an automatic before-and-after re-check.

- Knowledge base: 12 onboard protocols, 3 red-flag rules (head injury, anaphylaxis, heart attack) and a general algorithm; a catalog of 2,792 health problems with about 15,000 search phrasings; 363 life-threatening red flags.

- Built for a long mission: a pharmacy forecast until the end of the mission with allergy substitutes; a simple mode when the medical officer is the patient; graded 2-minute training alarms; a crew guardian that isolates a leak and supplies oxygen if the crew stops responding; a reaction test before docking.

HOW IT WORKS

A one-second simulation drives a physiology model for each person; scenarios change it (CO2 build-up, the medic falls ill, arrhythmia, decompression, kidney colic, solar flare, depressurization). In the exam, free text is matched to the catalog and a rule-based engine scores each protocol from complaints, sensors, context, answers and the daily check-in. A protocol is named only with enough evidence; when two options are close, the more dangerous one sets the urgency.

HOW IT ANSWERS THE CHALLENGE

All six suggested indicators are tracked: heart rate, blood pressure and body temperature continuously; blood sugar, sleep hours and mood in the daily check-in, each with color-coded limits that change decisions. Every scenario is mapped to one of NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Decisions on board in seconds instead of waiting up to 44 minutes for Earth; every decision is explainable; it covers the crew when the medic is the patient. The same tool fits polar stations, ships at sea and remote clinics. Next: real Bluetooth sensors, camera pulse (rPPG), an offline language model, clinical review.

VALIDATION

10 of 10 scenario complaints reach the right protocol; 30 of 30 free complaints in Ukrainian and English get a safe decision; 0 network requests. Engineering validation, not clinical.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS, JavaScript (no libraries); any modern browser; headless Chrome and ffmpeg for the videos; GitHub Pages hosting. Vital signs are simulated. Not a medical device.

Source code: https://github.com/Kalagan1337/asklepios
